Runoff of organic matter from disturbed areas could also increase the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and nutrient content of Howard Creek and portions of Lake Jocassee. Nutrients in great enough quantities could increase productivity locally in Lake Jocassee and in Howard Creek. Runoff could also alter the present dissolved solids content of Howard Creek by leaching of minerals from exposed soils. Due to the low buffering capacity of the water in Howard Creek and Lake Jocassee, the addition of acidic or basic materials could change the pH of the water. Run-off from exposed areas would have similar effects, being most critical in areas with acidic soils. The waters involved tend naturally to be slightly acidic and are near the lower end of the optimal range of pH values for aquatic life.
Leaching from exposed and inundated soils could result in some increase in mercury in Lake Jocassee. Although insufficient data are available to quantify this impact it is expected that such leaching would have an insignificant affect on water quality.
Depressions or pot holes formed during construction that collect water and sediment traps used to control turbidity could provide breeding places for mosquitos and other nuisance insects.
Releases of petroleum products resulting from fuel spills or improper disposal of used crankcase oil could have a severe impact on the aquatic habitat should these substances reach streams in the project area.
Applicant has proposed to process domestic wastes by use of a portable sewage treatment plant. The plant would have a capacity of about 15,000 gallons per day. Located at the east end of the construction yard, discharge from this facility would be made into Lake Jocassee at the confluence of the Whitewater River. This discharge would increase the annual nutrient loading to Lake Jocassee by an estimated 160 kg per of phosphorus 
(0.005 \text{ g/m}^2/\text{yr.})
 and 373 kg per of nitrogen 
(0.012 \text{ g/m}^2/\text{yr.})
. The discharge could cause a local increase in the nutrient levels in the Whitewater River cove and would also create an increase in Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD).
